items.text: Start the event loop once, with `asyncio.run(main())`
Async helps with waiting (network, disk), not heavy computation
Never call blocking code like `time.sleep()` inside a coroutine

scenes.question: An API replies with status `429`. What does it mean, and what should your code do?
options: The URL is wrong: fix it
Too many requests: wait, then retry
scenes.explain: 429 means you hit a **rate limit**. Wait (often the response says how long), then retry. Module 2 implements this with backoff.

captions.text: Every language model you will use in this course lives behind a web API.
You send an HTTP request, and you wait for the answer.
This lesson gives you the three tools that make that work well: type hints, HTTP
requests with httpx, and async and await.
You will annotate functions with type hints, and check them with a type checker.
Understand HTTP requests, responses, and status codes.
Call web APIs with httpx, including timeouts and error handling.
And run slow operations at the same time with async and await.
A type hint is a label saying what type a value should be.
After each parameter you write a colon and a type, and after the parentheses an
arrow and the return type.
This function takes a list of floats and returns a float.
Here, the dictionary maps strings to floats, and the vertical bar means or.
The function returns a float, or None when the model isn't found.
Called correctly, everything works as you'd expect.
But here's the important part.
Python does not enforce hints when the code runs.
Passing a string is allowed, and it only crashes deep inside the function.
Running it: two good results, and then a confusing type error from inside sum, far
away from the real mistake.
A type checker like mypy reads your hints without running the code, and points at
the exact line with the wrong argument, before you ever run it.
Your editor uses the same hints for autocompletion.
The simple types: str, int, float, and bool.
Collections say what's inside: a list of strings, or a dictionary from strings to
ints.
A vertical bar with None means the value might be missing.
A tuple hint lists each position, like a string and an int.
In Module 3, a library called Pydantic will use exactly these hints to validate real
data at runtime.
That's where hints become really powerful.
HTTP is the language of web APIs, and it is simpler than it sounds.
There are two sides: a client, which is your Python code, and a server, such as a
model provider's API.
The client sends a request.
It has a method, such as GET to read or POST to send data, a URL, headers with extra
information like your API key, and sometimes a body.
The server sends back a response: a status code saying how it went, headers, and a
body, which for AI APIs is almost always JSON.
Codes in the two hundreds mean success.
Two hundred is OK, two oh one is created.
Four hundreds mean the problem is on your side.
Bad input, a missing or wrong API key, or a URL that doesn't exist.
Retrying won't help.
Fix the request.
Four twenty-nine deserves its own card.
It means you hit a rate limit.
Every model API has them, and Module 2 shows how to wait and retry properly.
And five hundreds mean the server had a problem.
Those are often temporary, so a careful retry can succeed.
Now let's make real requests.
So that this works offline, I'm serving the project's sample data from a small local
web server, using Python's built-in http dot server.
httpx dot get sends a GET request and returns a response object.
Always pass a timeout.
A network call that hangs forever will freeze your agent.
The response tells us the status code and the content type header.
Raise for status turns any error status into an exception, so failures can't slip by
unnoticed.
Then dot json parses the body into Python objects.
And here we request a file that doesn't exist, and catch the HTTP status error to
read its status code.
First, start the local server in the background.
It serves the files in the data folder.
Then run the script.
Status two hundred with a JSON content type, ten records loaded, and a clean four oh
four for the missing file.
A language model call can take several seconds, and during that time your program is
just waiting for the network.
If an agent needs three independent answers and asks for them one by one, the waits
add up.
Three calls of one second each take three seconds.
With async, you start all three, wait for them together, and finish in about one
second.
That's not more computing power.
It's simply not wasting time waiting.
Async def defines a coroutine, a function that can pause.
Await means: pause here until this finishes, and let other work run meanwhile.
asyncio dot sleep stands in for waiting on a network reply.
This version awaits each call in a loop, so they still run one after another.
This version passes all three to asyncio dot gather, which runs them concurrently
and returns the results in the same order you passed them.
Finally, asyncio dot run starts the event loop that drives coroutines.
We time both versions.
A real measurement.
Three seconds one by one, one second concurrently.
httpx has an async client too.
The fetch coroutine awaits the request and returns how many records came back.
Async with opens one shared client, and closes it properly afterwards.
Gather fetches every URL at the same time.
This is exactly how the project's fetch command works.
Both files downloaded concurrently: ten records and five records.
Await only works inside an async function.
Start the event loop once, at the top of your program, with asyncio dot run.
Async speeds up waiting, for the network or the disk.
It doesn't make heavy calculations faster.
And never call blocking code, like time dot sleep, inside a coroutine.
It freezes every other task.
Use the async version instead.
Quick check.
An API replies with status four twenty-nine.
What does it mean, and what should your code do?
Too many requests.
You hit a rate limit, so wait, then retry.
You'll implement this properly, with backoff, in Module 2.
Type hints document your intent, and a type checker verifies them before the code
runs.
HTTP is a request and a response, and the status code tells you how it went.
Use httpx with a timeout, and raise for status.
And use async, await, and gather to wait for many calls at once.
You now have every Python skill the project needs.
In the next lesson, we start building the Python AI Toolkit.
